title: Language Exchange Café: Meeting New People
summary: At a café language exchange, you trade languages with new people: you read their stickers, shake hands, say your first name and keep the talk going with follow-up questions and your own stories.

blocks.title: Introduction
paragraphs: Today we spend an evening at a language exchange in a café. We learn how the evening works, how to order and how to introduce yourself. Then we practise long conversations with new people.

items.prompt: Do you like meeting new people? Why or why not?
What do you usually say first when you meet someone new?
Which language would you like to practise with a native speaker?

blocks.title: Part 1: How a Language Exchange Works
paragraphs: A language exchange is a trade: you give something, and you get something back. You help someone with your language, and they help you with theirs. For example, you speak Japanese and want to practise English. So you look for an English speaker who wants to practise Japanese. Everyone is a teacher and a student at the same time.

In this lesson, you visit the Dutch Language Café in The Hague. The Hague is a city in the Netherlands. Every Thursday at 19:30, its language exchange starts. Every visitor gets a language sticker. You write your languages on it and wear it on your shirt. You write the languages you speak, and your native language is one of them. Your native language is the first language you learned as a child. You also write the languages you want to practise. Why a sticker? The room is full of strangers, people you do not know. With one look at a sticker, you know who can help you. A sticker also gives you your first question. Do you see Spanish on someone's sticker? Then ask: I see you study Spanish. Why?

At 20:00, the speed exchange starts. You talk with one person for 3 minutes. Then you move to the next person. You and your partner take turns choosing the language. First one of you chooses, then the other. This way, both people practise. Why only 3 minutes? In a short time, you meet many new people. You also find the people you want to talk to again. At 20:30, everyone sits down at language tables. For example, there is an English table and a Spanish table. At each table, people talk or play games in one language. At 21:10, you can change tables and try a new language.

blocks.title: Check: Part 1: How a Language Exchange Works

items.prompt: Why does every visitor wear a language sticker?
items.answer: So other people see their languages and know who can help them.

rows.term: Hi, I'm here for the language exchange.
rows.meaning: when you walk in, before anyone asks you
rows.example: Hi, I'm here for the language exchange. – Welcome! What's your name?

rows.meaning: to say your first language
rows.example: My native language is Spanish, and I want to practise Dutch.

rows.meaning: when you read someone's sticker
rows.example: I see you study French. Why? – My partner is French.

rows.meaning: when the person has no sticker
rows.example: Which languages do you speak? – Dutch and a little Japanese.

blocks.title: Part 2: Ordering at the Café
paragraphs: At the Dutch Language Café, a Thursday ticket costs €11. The ticket includes the snacks and the games: they are in the price. The snacks are popcorn, crisps and nuts. You can eat some at your table for free. But drinks are not included. You buy them at the bar from the bartender. The bartender is the person who works behind the bar. You buy food there too.

On the menu, you see a funny name: koffie verkeerd. In English, it means wrong coffee. Why wrong? A normal Dutch coffee has only a little milk. Koffie verkeerd has a lot of warm milk, often more than the coffee. So it is the wrong way around. It costs €4.00. If you are hungry, try an empanada. An empanada is small and baked, with food inside. Here, you choose cheese, meat or spinach inside. One empanada costs €6.50.

A bar is loud, and a menu has new words. When you do not understand, do not just say yes. Ask: Sorry, can you say that again? Or ask about the new word: What does spinach mean? At a language café, everyone is a student, so questions are normal. A short answer helps you get the right drink and the right food.

items.answer: Wrong coffee, because it has much more milk than a normal Dutch coffee.

rows.meaning: to ask what your ticket pays for
rows.example: Are the snacks included? – Yes, popcorn, crisps and nuts. Drinks are not.

rows.example: Can I have a koffie verkeerd, please? – Sure, that's €4.00.

rows.meaning: to ask the price
rows.example: And the empanada? How much is it? – It's €6.50.

rows.term: Sorry, can you say that again?
rows.meaning: when you did not hear or understand

blocks.title: Part 3: Introducing Yourself
paragraphs: In the Netherlands, people shake hands when they meet someone new. At the same time, they say their name, often only the first name. Hi! I'm Sanne. In Japan, many people bow, or bend forward, and say their family name. The name is important. The Leiden International Centre helps people who move to the Netherlands. It says that a hello without your name is rude, or not polite. Why? Your name tells people who you are. It also tells them what to call you all evening. So when you hear a new name, say your name too. Then say: Nice to meet you.

At a first meeting, do not ask: How are you? For many Dutch people, it is a real question, not just a hello. They ask it when they really want to know the answer. So they usually ask people they already know. At a first meeting, just say hello and your name. Save How are you? for next Thursday, when you meet again.

In a 3-minute speed exchange, you do not have much time. So say three things: your name, your city and why you study the language. Daan says: Hi! I'm Daan. I live in The Hague. I study Japanese because I'm going to Tokyo in April. The last part is the most useful. It gives the other person a question. For example: What do you want to see in Tokyo? When you finish, ask back: What about you?

items.prompt: Why do Dutch people not ask How are you? at a first meeting?
items.answer: For them it is a real question, so they ask people they already know.

rows.meaning: after you hear a new name
rows.example: I'm Daan. – Nice to meet you, Daan. I'm Lucía.

rows.meaning: to say your city
rows.example: Where are you from? – I'm from Valencia, in Spain.

rows.meaning: to say your job. Say an when the first sound is a, e, i, o or u.
rows.example: What do you do? – I'm an engineer. – Oh, I'm a teacher.

rows.meaning: to say why you learn a language
rows.example: I study English because I want to travel.

rows.meaning: to ask the same question back
rows.example: I'm from Valencia. What about you? – I'm from The Hague.

blocks.title: Part 4: Keeping the Conversation Going
paragraphs: The best tool for a long conversation is the follow-up question. A follow-up question is a question about what the other person just said. Lucía says: I moved here from Valencia. A new question jumps to a new idea: Do you like football? A follow-up question stays with her idea: Why did you move here? She answers: For work. I work at a hotel. Now you take one part of her answer. Then you ask again: What do you do at the hotel? Each answer gives you the next question.

In 2017, scientists at Harvard University studied conversations between strangers. People who asked more questions were liked more by their partners. Follow-up questions worked best. Why? A follow-up question shows that you are really listening. But there is one problem. If you never talk about yourself, people may think you are hiding something. A good conversation goes both ways. React to what you hear, for example: Really? Me too! Or say: That sounds fun! Then tell something about yourself, and ask back.

At 21:30, the exchange ends. Do not just walk away: the other person gave you their time. Say: It was nice to talk to you. Do you want to keep in touch, or talk again later? Ask for WhatsApp. In the Netherlands, WhatsApp is by far the most used app for messages. Almost every phone there has it. So almost everyone you meet can say yes. The exchange is every Thursday, so you can also say: See you next Thursday!

rows.meaning: to keep in touch
rows.example: Can I add you on WhatsApp? – Sure! Here's my number.

rows.example: The exchange is over. – Bye, Lucía! See you next Thursday!

blocks.title: Scene: Arriving and Ordering
paragraphs: It is Thursday, 19:30. You walk into the Dutch Language Café, Herengracht 13A, in The Hague. You signed up online, and your ticket was €11. A host stands near the door with a box of stickers. After the host, you go to the bar. The bartender does not wear a sticker.
Your goal: get your sticker, then order a drink and food at the bar.
Phrases to use: Hi, I'm here for the language exchange. / Are the snacks included? / Can I have ... / What does ... mean?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Hi, I'm here for the language exchange.

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: Welcome! What's your name?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: I'm (your name). I signed up online.

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: Yes, here you are on my list. Is this your first time here?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Yes, it is.

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: Great, welcome! Where are you from?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: I'm from (your city), in Japan.

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: Oh, nice! Here's your sticker. Please write the languages you speak and the languages you want to practise.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: OK. My native language is Japanese, and I want to practise English.

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: Perfect. The speed exchange starts at 20:00.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Thank you. Are the snacks included?

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: Yes, the popcorn, crisps and nuts are in your ticket, and the games too. Drinks are not included. You buy them at the bar.

turns.speaker: Bartender
turns.text: Hi! What would you like?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Can I have a koffie verkeerd, please?

turns.speaker: Bartender
turns.text: Sure. Anything to eat?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: What is an empanada?

turns.speaker: Bartender
turns.text: It's small and baked, with food inside. We have cheese, meat or spinach.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Sorry, what does spinach mean?

turns.speaker: Bartender
turns.text: It's a green vegetable with soft leaves.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Ah, OK. A cheese one, please. How much is it?

turns.speaker: Bartender
turns.text: The koffie verkeerd is €4.00, and the empanada is €6.50. That's €10.50, please.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Here you go. Which languages do you speak?

turns.speaker: Bartender
turns.text: Dutch, English and some German. Enjoy the exchange!

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Thank you! Have a nice evening.

blocks.title: Scene: Meeting Your Table
paragraphs: It is 19:45. You sit down at a table with your coffee and your empanada. A Dutch woman sits next to you. Her sticker says: I speak Dutch and English. I practise Spanish. She smiles and holds out her hand.
Your goal: shake hands, say your name and get to know her.
Phrases to use: Nice to meet you / I'm from ... / I see you study ... / What about you?

turns.speaker: Sanne
turns.text: Hi! I'm Sanne.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Hi, Sanne! I'm (your name). Nice to meet you.

turns.speaker: Sanne
turns.text: Nice to meet you too. I see Japanese on your sticker. Where are you from?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: I'm from (your city), in Japan. What about you?

turns.speaker: Sanne
turns.text: I'm from here, The Hague. I come to this café every Thursday.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Every Thursday? Wow! I see you study Spanish. Why?

turns.speaker: Sanne
turns.text: I go to Spain every summer. I want to order food and talk to people in Spanish, not English!

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: That sounds fun! Is Spanish hard?

turns.speaker: Sanne
turns.text: Some parts, yes. The verbs are hard for me! And you? Why do you study English?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: I study English because (your reason for learning English).

turns.speaker: Sanne
turns.text: That's a great reason. What do you do?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: I'm a/an (your job). What about you?

turns.speaker: Sanne
turns.text: I'm a teacher. I teach children at a primary school.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Really? Do you like it?

turns.speaker: Sanne
turns.text: Yes, I love it. But on the weekend, I want a quiet day! What do you do in your free time?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: In my free time, I like (your hobby).

turns.speaker: Sanne
turns.text: Oh, nice! I play ping pong. There's a table here at the café. Do you play?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: A little. But I'm not very good!

turns.speaker: Sanne
turns.text: Me neither! Let's play later.

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: It's 20:00, everyone! The speed exchange starts now. Please find a partner.

turns.speaker: Sanne
turns.text: Oh, it's time! Good luck!

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Thanks, Sanne. See you later!

blocks.title: Scene: The Speed Exchange
paragraphs: It is 20:00. You talk with each person for 3 minutes. You and your partner take turns choosing the language. The room is full and loud. Your first partner's sticker says: I speak Dutch and English. I practise Japanese.
Your goal: speak English, then teach him a Japanese phrase for his trip.
Phrases to use: Nice to meet you / Sorry, can you say that again? / That sounds fun! / It was nice to talk to you

turns.speaker: Daan
turns.text: Hi! I'm Daan.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Hi, Daan! I'm (your name). Nice to meet you.

turns.speaker: Daan
turns.text: Nice to meet you too. We take turns choosing the language. You can choose first.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: English, please. I see Japanese on your sticker!

turns.speaker: Daan
turns.text: Yes, I study Japanese. I started six months ago, so I know only a little. What do you do?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: I'm a/an (your job). What about you?

turns.speaker: Daan
turns.text: I'm an engineer. I make machines for factories.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Sorry, can you say that again? It's very loud in here.

turns.speaker: Daan
turns.text: I'm an engineer. I make machines.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Oh, cool! Why do you study Japanese?

turns.speaker: Daan
turns.text: I'm going to Tokyo in April, for two weeks!

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: That sounds fun! What do you want to do there?

turns.speaker: Daan
turns.text: Eat a lot of ramen and see old temples. And you? Why do you study English?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: I study English because (your reason for learning English).

turns.speaker: Daan
turns.text: Good reason! OK, now it's my turn. Japanese, please. What can I say in a shop in Tokyo?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Say kore o hitotsu kudasai. It means this one, please.

turns.speaker: Daan
turns.text: Kore o... sorry, can you say that again?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Kore o hitotsu kudasai. Kore is this, hitotsu is one, and kudasai is please give me.

turns.speaker: Daan
turns.text: Kore o hitotsu kudasai! Is that right?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Yes, perfect! Point at the thing you want and say it.

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: Time's up! Please move to the next person.

turns.speaker: Daan
turns.text: Thank you! That's really useful.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: It was nice to talk to you, Daan. Have a great trip!

blocks.title: Scene: The English Table
paragraphs: It is 20:30. You sit at the English table, and Sanne is there too. A new woman sits down with you. Her sticker says: I speak Spanish and English. I practise Dutch. At 21:10, people can change tables, but you stay. The exchange ends at 21:30.
Your goal: ask follow-up questions, talk about yourself and keep in touch.
Phrases to use: Why did you move here? / How long have you lived here? / Really? Me too! / Can I add you on WhatsApp?

turns.speaker: Lucía
turns.text: Hi! I'm Lucía.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Hi, Lucía! I'm (your name). Nice to meet you. Where are you from?

turns.speaker: Lucía
turns.text: Nice to meet you too. I'm from Valencia, in Spain, but I moved to The Hague.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Really? Why did you move here?

turns.speaker: Lucía
turns.text: For work. I work at a big hotel.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Oh, nice! What do you do at the hotel?

turns.speaker: Lucía
turns.text: I work at the front desk. I say hello to the guests and give them their room keys.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: How long have you lived here?

turns.speaker: Lucía
turns.text: Two years. I study Dutch, but it's hard! And I miss the sun in Valencia.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: What is Valencia like?

turns.speaker: Lucía
turns.text: It's warm and sunny, and the food is great. What about you? What do you do?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: I'm a/an (your job). In my free time, I like (your hobby).

turns.speaker: Lucía
turns.text: Oh, nice! I see you study English. Why?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: I study English because (your reason for learning English).

turns.speaker: Lucía
turns.text: That's a great reason. Oh, you have a koffie verkeerd! I have one every Thursday. I really love coffee.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Really? Me too! It's my first koffie verkeerd, and it's very good.

turns.speaker: Lucía
turns.text: Next week, try the empanadas too!

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: I had a cheese one tonight. It was great!

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: It's 21:30, everyone. The exchange is over. Thank you for coming!

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: It was nice to talk to you, Lucía. Can I add you on WhatsApp?

turns.speaker: Lucía
turns.text: Sure! Here's my number. Let's practise again soon.

turns.speaker: Sanne
turns.text: Are you coming next Thursday?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Yes! See you next Thursday!

turns.speaker: Sanne
turns.text: See you next Thursday! Bye!

blocks.title: Speaking
paragraphs: Find a partner. One of you is the visitor. The other plays the host, the bartender, Sanne, Daan and Lucía. Replay the evening at the Dutch Language Café in time order. Say why you are here, and write your sticker. Order a koffie verkeerd and a cheese empanada for €10.50. Shake hands and give your real name, city, job and hobby. Say why you study English. Teach Daan one useful phrase in your language. Ask at least three follow-up questions. React with Really? Me too! or That sounds fun! At the end, ask for WhatsApp and say: See you next Thursday! Then change roles.

blocks.title: Final Reflection
blocks.intro: Follow-up questions and your own stories keep a language exchange going.

items.prompt: Would you like to go to a language exchange? Why or why not?
Someone says, I just started a new job. What follow-up question can you ask?
What three things will you say when you introduce yourself?
